lines.cap: **Narrator:** Term 3. Room 8H. Mr Hargreaves is on mug number sixteen, and carrying a very thick book.
**Mr H:** Right, 8H. This term: **the novel**.
**Will:** A **NOVEL**?! Three hundred pages of **PROSE**?! Where are the **iambs**?! Where are the swords?!
**Shady:** Relax, folks. I was there. Nobody panicked, Mr H wept with joy, and I saved everyone from a tiger.
**Mei:** Excuse me, trenchcoat guy — Mr H is drinking tea, and that's a ceiling fan, not a tiger.
**Omni:** Lady Omni, **omniscient narrator**. Through my binoculars I see Shady is lying, Mei wants a curry puff, and Will secretly envies Charles Dickens.
**Will:** Get out of my thought bubble, madam! I do NOT envy his book sales!
**Nib:** Remember: a novel is **constructed** prose fiction! Name the writer, and ask **WHAT, HOW, and WHY**.
**Mei:** Three hundred pages and a lying detective: **one star**.
**Narrator:** All the School's a Stage. Episode eleven: Unreliable.
**Narrator:** Tuesday. The library. Shady and Omni are arguing over who gets to narrate Mei's homework.
**Mr H:** Rule one: the **narrator** is NOT the **author**. Charlotte Brontë created Jane Eyre's voice; she wasn't locked in the red-room herself.
**Nib:** **First person** uses '**I**'. Intimate access to one mind, like Pip or Jane — yet limited and potentially biased.
**Mei:** **Second person** uses '**you**' — pointing the camera straight at the reader! Rare in whole novels, and slightly creepy.
**Mr H:** **Third person limited** uses 'he' or 'she', staying over **one** character's shoulder, like young Bruno in The Boy in the Striped Pyjamas.
**Omni:** **Third person omniscient** sees **every** mind, past and future, and comments openly! Listen to Dickens: '**Marley was dead: to begin with.**'
**Nib:** Some novels even switch between **multiple narrators**, like Wonder or Noughts and Crosses, so we compare sides.
**Shady:** Or pick me: an **unreliable narrator**! Maybe I'm **naïve**, **biased**, **deceptive**, or **remembering from long ago**!
**Mei:** Wait — when a naïve narrator misses the danger, **we** see what they don't! That's **dramatic irony**!
**Will:** Hark at Dickens's Great Expectations: 'the **small bundle of shivers** growing afraid of it all and beginning to cry, **was Pip**.'
**Nib:** A frightened boy wouldn't say 'bundle of shivers'! That's a **retrospective narrator**: child's terror in the adult Pip's wry words.
**Mr H:** Always explain both sides of perspective: what it **lets us feel**, and what it **hides**.
**Narrator:** Wednesday. Mr Hargreaves writes five letters on the whiteboard: S, T, E, A, L.
**Mr H:** **Direct characterisation** tells us outright. In The Secret Garden: 'the **most disagreeable-looking child** ever seen. It was true, too.'
**Nib:** **Indirect characterisation** **shows** us through **STEAL**: **Speech, Thoughts, Effect on others, Actions, and Looks**.
**Shady:** In Jekyll and Hyde, I barely bumped that kid — 'the man **trampled calmly** over the child's body.' Calmly! See? Polite!
**Mei:** 'Trampled **calmly**' is terrifying! The contrast between violence and zero emotion shows Hyde is inhuman!
**Will:** Listen to Dickens pile up verbs on Scrooge: 'a **squeezing, wrenching, grasping, scraping, clutching**, covetous, old sinner!'
**Omni:** And the simile: '**secret, and self-contained, and solitary as an oyster**.' Sibilant, hard shell — yet an oyster can hide a **pearl**!
**Nib:** Writers also pair a protagonist with a **foil character** — warm, cheerful Fred or Fezziwig makes Scrooge's icy greed look even sharper!
**Mr H:** A **dynamic** character changes across a **character arc** — **starting point**, **catalyst**, **end point** — whereas a **static** character stays the same.
**Nib:** And E. M. Forster separated one-note **flat** characters from complex **round** ones capable of surprising us!
**Mei:** Three spirits crack Scrooge's shell until he's '**as good a friend, as good a master, and as good a man**'! Two stars!
**Narrator:** Four p.m. Queenstown. Rain hammers the windows on schedule.
**Mr H:** **Setting** is place, time and social world. **Atmosphere** is the mood it creates for the reader.
**Omni:** Look inside Jane Eyre's **red-room**: 'deep red damask', 'crimson cloth', a bed 'like a **tabernacle**', a chair 'like a **pale throne**'.
**Mei:** Red connotes **anger**, **blood**, and **danger** — and 'throne' makes the furniture sit in judgement on ten-year-old Jane!
**Nib:** When weather or nature mirrors human emotion — mournful rain for grief, howling wind for turmoil — that is **pathetic fallacy**.
**Mr H:** Careful: when Dickens says 'No wind that blew was bitterer than' Scrooge, that's a **comparison**, not pathetic fallacy.
**Will:** Whereas Pip's 'bleak place overgrown with nettles' and 'dark flat wilderness' make the marshes threaten him before anyone speaks!
**Shady:** And in Jekyll and Hyde, my back door sits in 'a **blind forehead** of discoloured wall'! Totally welcoming, right?
**Omni:** Personifying a wall as '**blind**' turns the setting into a symbol of Victorian secrecy and hypocrisy.
**Mei:** So never just write 'the room is scary' — link setting to **character**, **tension**, or **symbolism**!
**Narrator:** Thursday. The school hall. Will has discovered cliffhangers and refuses to come down.
**Mr H:** **Plot** is what happens. **Structure** is how the writer arranges it: order, **pacing**, shifts and chapter endings.
**Nib:** **Freytag's pyramid** maps five stages — **Every Rocket Climbs, Falls, Returns**: **Exposition, Rising action, Climax, Falling action, Resolution**.
**Mei:** Wait — the **climax** isn't the very last page! Tension peaks first, then drops into falling action and **dénouement**!
**Omni:** Writers bend time too: **in medias res** drops us mid-action; **flashbacks** jump back; **foreshadowing** plants warnings!
**Nib:** And **circular structure** ends right where the novel began, like Of Mice and Men returning to the same river pool.
**Will:** Dickens published Great Expectations in **weekly instalments**! Every **cliffhanger** sold next week's magazine! Oh, I respect the hustle!
**Kevin:** Watch **pacing** in Chapter 1! One giant reflective sentence with six of my commas lullabies you across the churchyard...
**Shady:** '**Hold your noise!**' cried a terrible voice! Boom — short, violent imperative shatters the stillness!
**Mr H:** When analysing structure, track those shifts: **opens with**, **zooms in**, **interrupts**, **returns to** — and say **why**. Three stars!
**Narrator:** Friday. Room 8H. Essay day: writing about a **whole novel**.
**Mr H:** A one-word topic like 'loneliness' is just a **subject**. Phrase a **theme** as an **idea**: 'Burnett suggests being needed cures loneliness.'
**Nib:** A **motif** recurs across the novel, like cold and fire. A **symbol** is concrete standing for abstract, like the locked garden or Jekyll's 'blind' door.
**Mr H:** Weave in **context** only when it sharpens **writer's purpose**: in the 1843 Hungry Forties, Scrooge's workhouse line exposes real Victorian cruelty.
**Omni:** And don't quote only Chapter 1! Use **Then, Turn, The End**: evidence from the **beginning, turning point, and end**!
**Mei:** PEEL time! **Point**: Dickens presents Scrooge's greed as so extreme it physically freezes him.
**Mei:** **Evidence**: 'The **cold within him** froze his old features, **nipped** his pointed nose, **shrivelled** his cheek.'
**Mei:** **Explain**: The **extended metaphor** of inner cold and harsh verbs 'nipped' and 'shrivelled' imply greed harms Scrooge himself.
**Mei:** **Link**: Setting coldness up like weather prepares his Stave Five thaw, proving Dickens's message that anyone can choose generosity.
**Mr H:** Named the writer, zoomed on two verbs, linked to the whole-novel arc. Splendid.
**Narrator:** Before you close Chapter One, the department would like to save you some marks.
**Mei:** Memory hooks! **WHAT, HOW, WHY** on every extract; **STEAL** for indirect characterisation!
**Nib:** **Every Rocket Climbs, Falls, Returns** for Freytag's pyramid; **Then, Turn, The End** for whole-novel essays!
**Mr H:** One. Don't **retell the plot** or treat characters like real mates. Write '**Dickens presents**', '**Brontë suggests**'.
**Shady:** Two. Never confuse the **narrator** with the **author** — and watch out for **unreliable** narrators like me!
**Omni:** Three. Don't assume third person is always all-knowing: check **third limited** versus **omniscient**!
**Kevin:** Four. Don't quote only Chapter 1 in a whole-novel essay! Track **beginning, middle, and end**!
**Nib:** Five. State a **theme** as a full idea, not one word — and never bolt on random Victorian history!
**Will:** Six. Keep quotations **short and embedded**, like 'solitary as an oyster'. Even prose can turn a phrase.
**Mei:** Reading the Novel: **four stars**! Cliffhangers are sneaky, and Scrooge's oyster shell actually made sense.
**Will:** Four stars for **prose**?! My plays don't even have chapters!
**Mei:** Will, Hamlet is still four hours long.
**Mr H:** Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
**Mr H:** Which third-person perspective stays close to **one** character's thoughts rather than knowing everyone's?
**Omni:** **Third person limited** — also called close third person!
**Mr H:** What do the five letters of **STEAL** stand for in indirect characterisation?
**Mei:** **Speech, Thoughts, Effect on others, Actions, and Looks**.
**Mr H:** What technique uses **weather or nature** to mirror human emotion or mood?
**Nib:** **Pathetic fallacy**.
**Mr H:** Name the five stages of **Freytag's pyramid** in order.
**Kevin:** **Exposition, Rising action, Climax, Falling action, and Resolution**!
**Mr H:** In a whole-novel essay, from which **three parts** of the book should you choose quotations?
**Mr H:** The **beginning**, the **turning point** in the middle, and the **end**.
**Mr H:** Brilliant work. Now try the **Reading the Novel** quiz in your English Lab.
**Shady:** True story: Mei gave me six stars and bought me lunch.
**Omni:** Binoculars confirm: she gave four stars and ate the curry puff herself.
